claim: Presynaptic LAR family receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) regulate synapse development through mechanisms that include trans-synaptic adhesion.
source: Presynaptic LAR family receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) regulate synapse development through mechanisms that include trans-synaptic adhesion; however, whether they regulate postsynaptic receptor functions remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about LAR-RPTPs.

claim: Whether presynaptic LAR-RPTPs regulate postsynaptic receptor functions remains unknown.
source: Presynaptic LAR family receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) regulate synapse development through mechanisms that include trans-synaptic adhesion; however, whether they regulate postsynaptic receptor functions remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Presynaptic PTPσ enhances postsynaptic NMDA receptor (NMDAR) currents in the hippocampus.
source: Here we report that presynaptic PTPσ, a LAR-RPTP, enhances postsynaptic NMDA receptor (NMDAR) currents and NMDAR-dependent synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic PTPσ enhances NMDAR-dependent synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
source: Here we report that presynaptic PTPσ, a LAR-RPTP, enhances postsynaptic NMDA receptor (NMDAR) currents and NMDAR-dependent synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: PTPσ regulation of postsynaptic NMDAR function does not involve trans-synaptic adhesions of PTPσ.
source: This regulation does not involve trans-synaptic adhesions of PTPσ, suggesting that the cytoplasmic domains of PTPσ, known to have tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein-protein interactions, are important.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments with PTPσ mutants lacking extracellular adhesion capabilities.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of PTPσ, which have tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein-protein interactions, are important for regulating postsynaptic NMDAR function.
source: This regulation does not involve trans-synaptic adhesions of PTPσ, suggesting that the cytoplasmic domains of PTPσ, known to have tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein-protein interactions, are important.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that extracellular adhesion is not required, combined with knowledge about PTPσ domain functions.

claim: Phosphotyrosine levels of presynaptic proteins, including neurexin-1, are strongly increased in PTPσ-mutant mice.
source: In line with this, phosphotyrosine levels of presynaptic proteins, including neurexin-1, are strongly increased in PTPσ-mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Figure 4.

claim: PTPσ-dependent NMDAR regulation is important for social novelty recognition.
source: Behaviorally, PTPσ-dependent NMDAR regulation is important for social and reward-related novelty recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral experiments showing impaired social novelty recognition in mutant mice that is rescued by D-cycloserine.

claim: PTPσ-dependent NMDAR regulation is important for reward-related novelty recognition.
source: Behaviorally, PTPσ-dependent NMDAR regulation is important for social and reward-related novelty recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral experiments in Y-maze and Morris water maze tests.

claim: Presynaptic PTPσ regulates postsynaptic NMDAR function through trans-synaptic and direct adhesion-independent mechanisms.
source: These results suggest that presynaptic PTPσ regulates postsynaptic NMDAR function through trans-synaptic and direct adhesion-independent mechanisms and novelty recognition in social and reward contexts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the experimental findings.

claim: Neuroligin-1 regulates the synaptic localization and function of NMDARs.
source: For instance, the synaptic adhesion molecules neuroligin-1 (Budreck et al., 2013) and EphB2 (Dalva et al., 2000) regulate the synaptic localization and function of NMDARs.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Budreck et al., 2013).

claim: EphB2 regulates the synaptic localization and function of NMDARs.
source: For instance, the synaptic adhesion molecules neuroligin-1 (Budreck et al., 2013) and EphB2 (Dalva et al., 2000) regulate the synaptic localization and function of NMDARs.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Dalva et al., 2000).

claim: Neuroligin-1 acts through two distinct mechanisms to regulate NMDARs and long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: In addition, neuroligin-1 acts through two distinct mechanisms to regulate NMDARs and long-term potentiation (LTP) (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Wu et al., 2019).

claim: Presynaptic neurexin-3 promotes the postsynaptic localization of AMPARs by suppressing AMPAR endocytosis.
source: For example, presynaptic neurexin-3 promotes the postsynaptic localization of AMPARs by suppressing AMPAR endocytosis (Aoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Aoto et al., 2013).

claim: Alternative splicing of different neurexins distinctly regulates postsynaptic NMDAR- and AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: Alternative splicing of different neurexins also distinctly regulates postsynaptic NMDAR- and AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Dai et al., 2019).

claim: LAR-RPTPs are a family of synaptic organizers with three known members: LAR, PTPσ, and PTPδ.
source: LAR receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are a family of synaptic organizers with three known members (LAR, PTPσ, and PTPδ), each with a hybrid structure that includes a single-transmembrane domain, extracellular adhesion domains and intracellular domains D1 and D2 that possess protein tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein–protein interactions, respectively (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).

claim: LAR-RPTPs have a hybrid structure that includes a single-transmembrane domain, extracellular adhesion domains and intracellular domains D1 and D2.
source: LAR receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are a family of synaptic organizers with three known members (LAR, PTPσ, and PTPδ), each with a hybrid structure that includes a single-transmembrane domain, extracellular adhesion domains and intracellular domains D1 and D2 that possess protein tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein–protein interactions, respectively (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).

claim: The D1 domain of LAR-RPTPs possesses protein tyrosine phosphatase activity.
source: LAR receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are a family of synaptic organizers with three known members (LAR, PTPσ, and PTPδ), each with a hybrid structure that includes a single-transmembrane domain, extracellular adhesion domains and intracellular domains D1 and D2 that possess protein tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein–protein interactions, respectively (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).

claim: The D2 domain of LAR-RPTPs mediates protein-protein interactions.
source: LAR receptor tyrosine phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are a family of synaptic organizers with three known members (LAR, PTPσ, and PTPδ), each with a hybrid structure that includes a single-transmembrane domain, extracellular adhesion domains and intracellular domains D1 and D2 that possess protein tyrosine phosphatase activity and mediate protein–protein interactions, respectively (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic NGL-3.
source: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including NGL-3 (netrin-G ligand-3, also known as leucine-rich repeat-containing 4B [LRRC4B]) (Kwon et al., 2010; Woo et al., 2009), SALM3/5 (synaptic adhesion-like molecule 3/5, also known as leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type III domain containing 4 [LRFN4]) (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015), TrkC (tropomyosin receptor kinase C, also known as neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor type 3 [NTRK3]) (Takahashi et al., 2011), and Slitrks (SLIT and NTRK like) (Takahashi et al., 2012; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Kwon et al., 2010; Woo et al., 2009).

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic SALM3/5.
source: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including NGL-3 (netrin-G ligand-3, also known as leucine-rich repeat-containing 4B [LRRC4B]) (Kwon et al., 2010; Woo et al., 2009), SALM3/5 (synaptic adhesion-like molecule 3/5, also known as leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type III domain containing 4 [LRFN4]) (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015), TrkC (tropomyosin receptor kinase C, also known as neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor type 3 [NTRK3]) (Takahashi et al., 2011), and Slitrks (SLIT and NTRK like) (Takahashi et al., 2012; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic TrkC.
source: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including NGL-3 (netrin-G ligand-3, also known as leucine-rich repeat-containing 4B [LRRC4B]) (Kwon et al., 2010; Woo et al., 2009), SALM3/5 (synaptic adhesion-like molecule 3/5, also known as leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type III domain containing 4 [LRFN4]) (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015), TrkC (tropomyosin receptor kinase C, also known as neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor type 3 [NTRK3]) (Takahashi et al., 2011), and Slitrks (SLIT and NTRK like) (Takahashi et al., 2012; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi et al., 2011).

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic Slitrks.
source: Presynaptic LAR-RPTPs interact with postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including NGL-3 (netrin-G ligand-3, also known as leucine-rich repeat-containing 4B [LRRC4B]) (Kwon et al., 2010; Woo et al., 2009), SALM3/5 (synaptic adhesion-like molecule 3/5, also known as leucine-rich repeat and fibronectin type III domain containing 4 [LRFN4]) (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015), TrkC (tropomyosin receptor kinase C, also known as neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor type 3 [NTRK3]) (Takahashi et al., 2011), and Slitrks (SLIT and NTRK like) (Takahashi et al., 2012; Yim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Takahashi et al., 2012; Yim et al., 2013).

claim: LAR-RPTPs interact with cytoplasmic scaffolding/adaptor proteins including liprin-α, Trio and caskin to organize presynaptic protein complexes and promote functional differentiation.
source: In addition, LAR-RPTPs interact with cytoplasmic scaffolding/adaptor proteins, including liprin-α, Trio and caskin, to organize presynaptic protein complexes and promote functional differentiation (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Takahashi and Craig, 2013; Um and Ko, 2013).

claim: PTPσ regulates neurodevelopment, as evidenced by smaller brain, sensory-motor deficits and neuroendocrine defects in PTPσ-mutant mice.
source: In vivo studies on LAR-RPTP–mutant mice have revealed that PTPσ regulates neurodevelopment, as evidenced by the smaller brain, sensory-motor deficits and neuroendocrine defects in these mutant mice (Elchebly et al., 1999; Wallace et al., 1999); it also regulates learning and memory (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Elchebly et al., 1999; Wallace et al., 1999).

claim: PTPσ regulates learning and memory.
source: In vivo studies on LAR-RPTP–mutant mice have revealed that PTPσ regulates neurodevelopment, as evidenced by the smaller brain, sensory-motor deficits and neuroendocrine defects in these mutant mice (Elchebly et al., 1999; Wallace et al., 1999); it also regulates learning and memory (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Horn et al., 2012).

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed largely normal postnatal growth and survival, with a nearly normal Mendelian ratio of ~0.22.
source: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed largely normal postnatal growth and survival, with a nearly normal Mendelian ratio of ~0.22 (versus the expected 0.25) and postnatal body weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PTPσ global KO mice (Ptprs–l– mice) showed a strongly reduced Mendelian ratio (~0.15).
source: In contrast, PTPσ global KO mice (Ptprs–l– mice), generated in the present study, showed a strongly reduced Mendelian ratio (~0.15) and decreased body weight (~65% of WT at postnatal day [P] 21).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: PTPσ global KO mice showed decreased body weight (~65% of WT at postnatal day 21).
source: In contrast, PTPσ global KO mice (Ptprs–l– mice), generated in the present study, showed a strongly reduced Mendelian ratio (~0.15) and decreased body weight (~65% of WT at postnatal day [P] 21).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal walking patterns.
source: Unlike Ptprs–l– mice, which exhibited gait abnormalities, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal walking patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Ptprs–l– mice exhibited gait abnormalities.
source: Unlike Ptprs–l– mice, which exhibited gait abnormalities, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal walking patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The gross morphology of the brain of Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice was normal.
source: The gross morphology of the brain of Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice was normal, as revealed by staining with the nuclear marker DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PTPσ is widely distributed in various brain regions, including the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, and amygdala.
source: The distribution pattern of PTPσ in the brain, revealed by X-gal staining of PTPσ-mutant mice carrying the β-Geo cassette (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A for details), indicated widespread PTPσ distribution in various brain regions, including the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, and amygdala (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Excitatory neuron-restricted deletion of PTPσ minimally affects neurodevelopmental phenotypes.
source: These results suggest that excitatory neuron-restricted deletion of PTPσ, unlike global KO, minimally affects neurodevelopmental phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice and global KO mice.

claim: The frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) is normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: The frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) were normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) is normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: The frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) were normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The frequency of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) is normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: The frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) were normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) is normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: The frequency and amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) were normal in CA1 pyramidal neurons from Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Evoked EPSCs at Schaffer collateral-CA1 pyramidal cell (SC-CA1) synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice were comparable to those at wild-type (WT) synapses.
source: Evoked EPSCs at Schaffer collateral-CA1 pyramidal cell (SC-CA1) synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice were also comparable to those at wild-type (WT) synapses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation was normal at mutant SC-CA1 synapses.
source: In addition, paired-pulse facilitation, a measure of presynaptic function, was normal at mutant SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Excitatory neuron-restricted deletion of PTPσ does not affect spontaneous or evoked basal excitatory synaptic transmission at SC-CA1 synapses in mice.
source: These results suggest that excitatory neuron-restricted deletion of PTPσ does not affect spontaneous or evoked basal excitatory synaptic transmission at SC-CA1 synapses in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mEPSC, evoked EPSC, and paired-pulse facilitation data.

claim: Global PTPσ-null mice exhibit increased mEPSC frequency at SC-CA1 synapses.
source: These results differ from previous results obtained using global PTPσ-null mice, which exhibit increased mEPSC frequency and increased paired-pulse facilitation at SC-CA1 synapses (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Horn et al., 2012).

claim: Global PTPσ-null mice exhibit increased paired-pulse facilitation at SC-CA1 synapses.
source: These results differ from previous results obtained using global PTPσ-null mice, which exhibit increased mEPSC frequency and increased paired-pulse facilitation at SC-CA1 synapses (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Horn et al., 2012).

claim: LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation (HFS-LTP) was suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses compared with that at WT synapses.
source: LTP induced by high-frequency stimulation (HFS-LTP) was suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses compared with that at WT synapses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: LTP induced by theta-burst stimulation (TBS-LTP) was suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses.
source: Similarly, LTP induced by theta-burst stimulation (TBS-LTP) was suppressed at these synapses (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: LTD induced by low-frequency stimulation (LFS-LTD) was suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses.
source: Intriguingly, LTD induced by low-frequency stimulation (LFS-LTD) was also suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1G), a result that contrasts with a previous report that LFS-LTD at these synapses is normal in global PTPσ-KO mice (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: LFS-LTD at SC-CA1 synapses is normal in global PTPσ-KO mice.
source: Intriguingly, LTD induced by low-frequency stimulation (LFS-LTD) was also suppressed at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1G), a result that contrasts with a previous report that LFS-LTD at these synapses is normal in global PTPσ-KO mice (Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Horn et al., 2012).

claim: Metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD induced by the group I mGluR agonist DHPG was normal at mutant synapses.
source: In contrast, metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD induced by the group I mGluR agonist DHPG was normal at mutant synapses (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: The ratio of NMDAR-EPSCs and AMPAR-EPSCs (NMDA/AMPA ratio) was decreased at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses.
source: Indeed, the ratio of NMDAR-EPSCs and AMPAR-EPSCs (NMDA/AMPA ratio) was decreased at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: The decrease in NMDAR currents at Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl SC-CA1 synapses is mediated by the GluN2B subunit of NMDARs.
source: This result, together with the normal levels of basal excitatory synaptic transmission and mEPSCs, mediated by AMPARs, suggest that NMDAR currents are selectively decreased.
evidence: This is inferred from the decay kinetics of NMDAR EPSCs shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Levels of the GluN2B subunit were most strongly decreased in crude synaptosomal (P2) and PSD fractions of the Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampus.
source: Indeed, levels of the GluN2B subunit were most strongly decreased in crude synaptosomal (P2) and PSD fractions, but not in the total lysates, of the Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampus (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunoblot analysis, supported by data in Figure 1J.

claim: D-cycloserine fully rescued the NMDA/AMPA ratio at SC-CA1 synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampal slices.
source: D-cycloserine fully rescued the NMDA/AMPA ratio and TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampal slices without affecting the NMDA/AMPA ratio or TBS-LTP at WT SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings with D-cycloserine treatment, supported by data in Figure 1K.

claim: D-cycloserine fully rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampal slices.
source: D-cycloserine fully rescued the NMDA/AMPA ratio and TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampal slices without affecting the NMDA/AMPA ratio or TBS-LTP at WT SC-CA1 synapses (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings with D-cycloserine treatment, supported by data in Figure 1L.

claim: The decreased LTP and LTD in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice mainly involve decreased NMDAR currents rather than signaling pathways downstream of NMDAR activation.
source: In addition, considering the extents of the decreases in HFS-LTP, TBS-LTP, and LFS-LTD (~44%,~66%, and ~53%, respectively) and the decrease in the NMDA/AMPA ratio (~45%) at the mutant synapses under naïve and D-cycloserine rescue conditions (Figure 1E–I and K,L), the decreased LTP and LTD seem to mainly involve decreased NMDAR currents rather than signaling pathways downstream of NMDAR activation.
evidence: This is inferred from quantitative comparison of the extent of LTP/LTD suppression and NMDAR current reduction, and the rescue by D-cycloserine.

claim: Cre-induced deletion of PTPσ in the CA3 region suppresses TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: LTP experiments indicated that Cre-induced deletion of PTPσ in the CA3 region suppresses TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in Ptprsfl/fl mice compared with control synapses expressing EGFP alone (no Cre) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings after region-specific viral injection, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of PTPσ in the CA1 region had no effect on TBS-LTP.
source: In contrast, deletion of PTPσ in the CA1 region had no effect on TBS-LTP.
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings after region-specific viral injection, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: PTPσ in the presynaptic (CA3) region, but not the postsynaptic (CA1) region, is important for normal LTP at SC-CA1 synapses.
source: These results suggest that PTPσ in the presynaptic (CA3) region, but not the postsynaptic (CA1) region, is important for normal LTP at SC-CA1 synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the region-specific deletion experiments.

claim: Re-expression of WT PTPσ in the CA3 region of Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses.
source: Re-expression of WT PTPσ in the CA3 region of Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice by local injection of AAV-eIF1a-Ptprs rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses, restoring it to levels comparable to those in Ptprsfl/fl (control) mice injected with control virus (AAV-hSyn-eGFP) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings after viral rescue, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: Acute presynaptic re-expression of PTPσ in CA3 rescues postsynaptic LTP in the CA1 region.
source: These results suggest that acute presynaptic re-expression of PTPσ in CA3 rescues postsynaptic LTP in the CA1 region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the viral rescue experiments.

claim: Re-expression of PTPσ mutants lacking HSPG/CSPG or Slitrk1/TrkC interactions in the CA3 region rescued TBS-LTP to an extent similar to that of WT PTPσ injection.
source: Surprisingly, re-expression of either PTPσ mutant in the CA3 region by local AAV injection rescued TBS-LTP to an extent similar to that of WT PTPσ injection (Figure 3E), suggesting that HSPG/CSPG and Slitrk1 interactions are not important for the rescue of LTP.
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings after viral rescue with mutant PTPσ, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: HSPG/CSPG and Slitrk1 interactions are not important for the rescue of LTP by PTPσ.
source: Surprisingly, re-expression of either PTPσ mutant in the CA3 region by local AAV injection rescued TBS-LTP to an extent similar to that of WT PTPσ injection (Figure 3E), suggesting that HSPG/CSPG and Slitrk1 interactions are not important for the rescue of LTP.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with PTPσ mutants lacking these interactions.

claim: PTPσ mutants containing deletions of Ig1+2, Ig3, or FNIII1-2 domains rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in the Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampus when re-expressed in the CA3 region.
source: However, all of these PTPσ mutants rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in the Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampus when re-expressed in the CA3 region, although the PTPσ mutant containing an Ig3 deletion produced only partial rescue (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings after viral rescue with domain-deleted PTPσ mutants, supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: The PTPσ mutant containing an Ig3 deletion produced only partial rescue of TBS-LTP.
source: However, all of these PTPσ mutants rescued TBS-LTP at SC-CA1 synapses in the Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl hippocampus when re-expressed in the CA3 region, although the PTPσ mutant containing an Ig3 deletion produced only partial rescue (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: The extracellular domains or regions of PTPσ are not important for PTPσ-dependent postsynaptic regulation of LTP.
source: These results collectively suggest that the extracellular domains or regions of PTPσ are not important for PTPσ-dependent postsynaptic regulation of LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with various PTPσ extracellular mutants.

claim: Of 1549 proteins (3894 pTyr motifs), 57 proteins (80 pTyr motifs) showed significant changes in pTyr levels in mutant mice compared with WT mice.
source: This proteomic analysis revealed that, of 1549 proteins (3894 pTyr motifs), 57 proteins (80 pTyr motifs) showed significant changes in pTyr levels in mutant mice compared with WT mice (p<0.05; fold change >1.5), as indicated by a volcano plot (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from proteomic analysis, supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: 29 proteins showed upregulation of pTyr levels in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: These significant changes included both upregulation (29 proteins/33 motifs) and downregulation (29 proteins/47 motifs) of pTyr levels.
evidence: This is a direct observation from proteomic analysis.

claim: 29 proteins showed downregulation of pTyr levels in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: These significant changes included both upregulation (29 proteins/33 motifs) and downregulation (29 proteins/47 motifs) of pTyr levels.
evidence: This is a direct observation from proteomic analysis.

claim: GluN2B showed altered phosphorylation at tyrosine residues 985, 997, 1004, 1367 and 1369 in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Proteins of particular interest among those that were differentially tyrosine phosphorylated include the GluN2B subunit of NMDARs with altered phosphorylation at tyrosine residues 985, 997, 1004, 1367 and 1369.
evidence: This is a direct observation from proteomic analysis.

claim: TrkC was differentially phosphorylated at tyrosine residues 597 and 604 in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Another protein of interest was TrkC, a postsynaptic adhesion partner of PTPσ (Takahashi et al., 2011) that was found to be differentially phosphorylated at tyrosine residues 597 and 604.
evidence: This is a direct observation from proteomic analysis.

claim: GO terms with the strongest scores for proteins with significant pTyr changes were synapse related, including 'synapse', 'excitatory synapse' and 'postsynaptic specialization'.
source: A DAVID Gene Ontology (GO) analysis (http:// david.ncifcrf.gov) of proteins with significant pTyr levels showed that GO terms in the cellular compartment module with the strongest scores were synapse related, and included 'synapse', 'excitatory synapse' and 'postsynaptic specialization' (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct result from DAVID GO analysis, supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Upregulated pTyr proteins were more enriched at presynaptic than postsynaptic sites (9 presynaptic and four postsynaptic).
source: Intriguingly, upregulated proteins were more enriched at presynaptic than postsynaptic sites (9 presynaptic and four postsynaptic) (Figure 4E), whereas downregulated proteins were more strongly enriched at postsynaptic than presynaptic sites (15 postsynaptic and 0 presynaptic) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a direct result from SynGO analysis, supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: Downregulated pTyr proteins were more strongly enriched at postsynaptic than presynaptic sites (15 postsynaptic and 0 presynaptic).
source: Intriguingly, upregulated proteins were more enriched at presynaptic than postsynaptic sites (9 presynaptic and four postsynaptic) (Figure 4E), whereas downregulated proteins were more strongly enriched at postsynaptic than presynaptic sites (15 postsynaptic and 0 presynaptic) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a direct result from SynGO analysis, supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Presynaptic proteins showed mainly increased pTyr levels in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Volcano plot displays of these pre- and postsynaptic proteins, determined based on the SynGO analysis, further highlighted the fact that presynaptic proteins showed mainly increased pTyr levels, whereas postsynaptic proteins showed mainly decreased pTyr levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from volcano plot analysis, supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Postsynaptic proteins showed mainly decreased pTyr levels in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Volcano plot displays of these pre- and postsynaptic proteins, determined based on the SynGO analysis, further highlighted the fact that presynaptic proteins showed mainly increased pTyr levels, whereas postsynaptic proteins showed mainly decreased pTyr levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from volcano plot analysis, supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Deletion of PTPσ has minimal impacts on the synaptic localization of PTPσ-related proteins.
source: These results suggest that deletion of PTPσ has minimal impacts on the synaptic localization of PTPσ-related proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunoblot analysis showing no changes in synaptic levels of various PTPσ-related proteins.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice failed to recognize the novel object in the novel object-recognition test.
source: Unlike WT mice, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice failed to recognize the novel object on day 2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal social approach in the three-chamber test.
source: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal social approach, as indicated by the preference for a social target (stranger mouse) over an object, but failed to show normal social novelty preference, similarly exploring new and old stranger mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice failed to show normal social novelty preference in the three-chamber test.
source: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal social approach, as indicated by the preference for a social target (stranger mouse) over an object, but failed to show normal social novelty preference, similarly exploring new and old stranger mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice spent increasingly less time with the initial stranger mouse over the first four days in the modified social interaction test.
source: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice spent increasingly less time with the initial stranger mouse over the first four days, indicative of normal social cognition and habituation, but spent less time with a novel mouse on day five compared with WT mice (Figure 5C), further confirming the decrease in social-novelty recognition.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice spent less time with a novel mouse on day five in the modified social interaction test compared with WT mice.
source: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice spent increasingly less time with the initial stranger mouse over the first four days, indicative of normal social cognition and habituation, but spent less time with a novel mouse on day five compared with WT mice (Figure 5C), further confirming the decrease in social-novelty recognition.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice displayed less efficient switching to the novel arm containing the reward on day 2 in the Y-maze test.
source: In the Y-maze test, where the reward arm on day one was switched to another arm on day 2, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice displayed less efficient switching to the novel arm containing the reward on day 2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal learning and memory in the initial phase of the Morris water maze test.
source: Lastly, in the Morris water maze test, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice showed normal learning and memory in the initial phase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: In the reversal phase of the Morris water maze test, Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice were less efficient in switching to the novel platform location.
source: However, in the reversal phase, in which the location of the hidden platform was switched to a new quadrant, the mutant mice were less efficient in switching to the novel platform location (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice display decreases in the ability to recognize a novel object, a novel social target, a novel reward-arm location and a novel platform location.
source: These results indicate that Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice display decreases in the ability to recognize a novel object (novel-object recognition test), a novel social target (three-chamber test), a novel reward-arm location (Y-maze test) and a novel platform location (Morris water maze), collectively suggesting that the mutant mice have suppressed novelty recognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple behavioral tests.

claim: Acute treatment with D-cycloserine (20 mg/kg; i.p.) rescued social-novelty recognition deficits in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Acute treatment with the NMDAR agonist D-cycloserine (20 mg/kg; i.p.) rescued social-novelty recognition deficits in Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice, as assessed using the three-chamber test, without affecting social-novelty recognition in WT mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing with drug treatment, supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: D-cycloserine had no effect on social approach in WT or Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: In addition, D-cycloserine had no effect on social approach in WT or Emx1-Cre;Ptprsfl/fl mice.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing with drug treatment, supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Cre-induced PTPσ deletion in the CA3 region resulted in impaired social-novelty recognition in Ptprsfl/fl mice in the three-chamber test.
source: Cre-induced PTPσ deletion in the CA3 region resulted in impaired social-novelty recognition in Ptprsfl/fl mice in the three-chamber test compared with control Ptprsfl/fl mice expressing EGFP alone, without affecting social approach (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing after region-specific viral injection, supported by data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Cre-induced PTPσ deletion in the CA1 region had no effect on social-novelty recognition or social approach.
source: In contrast, Cre-induced PTPσ deletion in the CA1 region had no effect on social-novelty recognition or social approach.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing after region-specific viral injection, supported by data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Cre-induced deletion of PTPσ in the CA3 region impaired recognition of the novel reward arm location in the Y-maze test in Ptprsfl/fl mice.
source: Cre-induced deletion of PTPσ in the CA3 region also impaired recognition of the novel reward arm location in the Y-maze test in Ptprsfl/fl mice compared with control Ptprsfl/fl mice expressing EGFP alone (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing after region-specific viral injection, supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: Deletion of presynaptic, but not postsynaptic, PTPσ impairs social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition in adult mice.
source: These results suggest that deletion of presynaptic, but not postsynaptic, PTPσ impairs social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition in adult mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from region-specific deletion experiments.

claim: WT mice injected in the CA1 region with AAV-pU6-shGluN1 displayed suppressed social-novelty recognition in the three-chamber test.
source: WT mice (C57BL/6J) injected in the CA1 region with AAV-pU6-shGluN1 displayed suppressed social-novelty recognition, but normal social approach, in the three-chamber test (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing after GluN1 knockdown, supported by data in Figure 6E,F.

claim: WT mice injected in the CA1 region with AAV-pU6-shGluN1 failed to recognize the novel reward-arm location in the Y-maze test.
source: In addition, WT mice injected in the CA1 region with AAV-pU6-shGluN1 failed to recognize the novel reward-arm location in the Y-maze test, whereas control WT mice similarly injected with AAV-pU6-shCtrl showed no such change (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing after GluN1 knockdown, supported by data in Figure 6G.

claim: Normal expression of NMDARs in the CA1 region is important for social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition.
source: Therefore, normal expression of NMDARs in the CA1 region is important for social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from GluN1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Presynaptic PTPσ-mediated regulation of postsynaptic NMDAR currents and NMDAR-dependent LTP is important for social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition in mice.
source: These results collectively suggest that presynaptic PTPσ-mediated regulation of postsynaptic NMDAR currents and NMDAR-dependent LTP is important for social novelty and novel reward-arm recognition in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including D-cycloserine rescue, region-specific deletion, and GluN1 knockdown experiments.

claim: The decreased synaptic levels of GluN2B at mutant excitatory synapses may partly contribute to the decreased NMDAR currents.
source: Our data suggest that the decreased synaptic levels of GluN2B at mutant excitatory synapses, supported by immunoblot analysis of synaptic proteins and the faster decay kinetics of NMDAR currents, may partly contribute to the decreased NMDAR currents, which in turn seems to underlie the reduced LTP, based on quantitative comparisons.
evidence: This is inferred from immunoblot data and NMDAR current kinetics.

claim: Neurexin-1 promotes NMDAR-mediated, but not AMPAR-mediated, postsynaptic responses.
source: Among these proteins, presynaptic neurexin-1, but not neurexins 2/3, promotes NMDAR-mediated, but not AMPAR-mediated, postsynaptic responses (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Dai et al., 2019).

claim: PTPσ may contribute to the neurexin-1–dependent regulation of postsynaptic NMDARs.
source: Therefore, PTPσ, which is linked to neurexin-1 through liprin-α and CASK (Hata et al., 1996; Olsen et al., 2005; Serra-Pagès et al., 1995) or caskin (Bomkamp et al., 2019; Weng et al., 2011), may contribute to the neurexin-1–dependent regulation of postsynaptic NMDARs.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing increased neurexin-1 phosphorylation and known protein interactions.

claim: LTP can be regulated by EphA4.
source: For instance, LTP can be regulated by EphA4 (Filosa et al., 2009), APP (Weyer et al., 2011), and synaptotagmin-11 (Shimojo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Filosa et al., 2009).

claim: LTP can be regulated by APP.
source: For instance, LTP can be regulated by EphA4 (Filosa et al., 2009), APP (Weyer et al., 2011), and synaptotagmin-11 (Shimojo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Weyer et al., 2011).

claim: LTP can be regulated by synaptotagmin-11.
source: For instance, LTP can be regulated by EphA4 (Filosa et al., 2009), APP (Weyer et al., 2011), and synaptotagmin-11 (Shimojo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Shimojo et al., 2019).

claim: Hippocampal LTD but not LTP has been associated with novel-object/feature recognition in a space.
source: In addition, hippocampal LTD but not LTP has been associated with novel-object/feature recognition in a space (Dong et al., 2012; Kemp and Manahan-Vaughan, 2004; Kemp and Manahan-Vaughan, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Dong et al., 2012; Kemp and Manahan-Vaughan, 2004; Kemp and Manahan-Vaughan, 2007).

claim: Deletion of all three LAR-RPTPs (PTPσ, PTPδ, and LAR) minimally affects synapse development but critically regulates postsynaptic NMDAR, but not AMPAR, responses by a trans-synaptic mechanism.
source: Lastly, a recent paper has reported that deletion of all three LAR-RPTPs (PTPσ, PTPδ, and LAR) minimally affects synapse development but critically regulate postsynaptic NMDAR, but not AMPAR, responses by a trans-synaptic mechanism (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).

claim: PTPδ and LAR, in addition to PTPσ, participate in the regulation of trans-synaptic NMDAR regulation.
source: This study also extends our study by finding that PTPδ and LAR, in addition to PTPσ, participate in the regulation of trans-synaptic NMDAR regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited study (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).
